topic: CO2 is not carried predominantly as carbonic acid
issue: Slide says “Carbonic Acid (H2CO3) – 70%”, but most CO2 is transported as bicarbonate (HCO3−) formed after H2CO3 dissociates. Preserve the lecturer’s ~70/23/7 proportions as approximate but label the chemistry correctly.
handling: Explain carbonic anhydrase catalysis, H2CO3 as transient intermediate, HCO3− in plasma and chloride shift. Do not teach “70% carbonic acid” as literal final form.

issue: Slide calls CO2-bound blood blue; actual venous blood remains red (usually darker). Blue in diagrams is a convention.
handling: Retain oxyhemoglobin/carbaminohemoglobin vocabulary, but explicitly correct blue-blood misconception.

topic: The term external respiration is defined broadly in the lecture
issue: Lecture labels ventilation, pulmonary gas exchange and transport together as “external respiration”, while many texts reserve external respiration for pulmonary capillary gas exchange.
handling: Teach the three steps exactly as a course framework, then state textbook usage differs.

topic: Nasal nitric oxide and breathing benefits may be overstated
issue: Slides attribute better diffusion and oxygen uptake to nasal breathing/NO without conditions or quantitative support; not all are established as simple universal benefits.
handling: Lead with grounded warming/humidification/filtration/olfaction; describe NO as possible physiological influence, not a guaranteed major boost to oxygen uptake.

topic: Airway histology varies within broad regions
issue: The whole pharynx is not uniformly stratified squamous; nasopharynx commonly has respiratory mucosa, and nasal vestibule has squamous epithelium. Bronchioles transition in lining.
handling: Keep lecture shortcut for memorization with a short anatomical exception note.

topic: Epiglottis does not provide the only airway protection
issue: Swallowing-related laryngeal elevation, aryepiglottic structures and true/false fold closure all participate; epiglottis is not a lone mechanical door.
handling: Explain multiple coordinated protections without belaboring it in Exam Cram.

topic: A rise or fall of one mmHg is an illustrative example
issue: Atmospheric 760 and alveolar 759/761 mmHg depict an idealized near-sea-level situation, not fixed universal respiratory pressures.
handling: State the pressure difference and direction matter; absolute atmospheric pressure varies with elevation.

topic: Boyle law needs constant temperature and amount of gas assumptions
issue: Slide presents P=1/V without proportionality constant or assumptions.
handling: Use P∝1/V, or P1V1=P2V2 at constant gas amount and temperature; distinguish the lung’s open airflow from simplified closed gas model.

issue: Apneustic/pneumotaxic centers are useful exam labels but modern control circuitry is distributed; pre-Bötzinger and pontine respiratory groups matter.
handling: Preserve DRG/VRG, apneustic, pneumotaxic exam associations; label modern framework as further scientific context.

topic: Quiet and forced breathing classifications are simplified
issue: Slides equate forced breathing with hyperpnea and VRG as active only in forced breathing. Hyperpnea is increased ventilation, which is not exactly the same as active expiration; VRG includes rhythm-generating networks.
handling: Follow course language for exam while clarifying broader physiology in Deep Dive.

topic: Bronchoconstriction/bronchodilation is more complex than a single nerve pathway
issue: Simplified sympathetic-versus-parasympathetic language is valid instructional shorthand; bronchial smooth muscle also responds to circulating epinephrine, local mediators and inflammation.
handling: Retain receptor-level autonomic overview, clearly mark immune/local mediators as extension.

topic: Residual volume and direct spirometric measurement
issue: RV remains after maximal expiration and ordinary spirometry cannot directly obtain it; VC and TLC should be expressed as combinations of basic volumes.
handling: Make a concise table and equation set in the Deep Dive; course slides alone do not teach measurement methods in detail.

issue: Carbaminohemoglobin describes CO2 binding to hemoglobin, but not the primary transport form of CO2. Oxygen unloads in tissues in response to pO2 and also pH/CO2-dependent affinity.
handling: Avoid implying hemoglobin binds O2 and CO2 competitively at exactly the same group; include Bohr-effect caveat.

issue: Slide uses “apoxia”; “anoxia” is more commonly used for severe/absent oxygen supply. Instructor may expect slide terminology.
handling: Present the original term as used in lecture, note conventional anoxia terminology without silently changing source.

topic: Nasal vs lung exposure benefits and respiratory portion boundary
issue: Slides define respiratory portion as “smallest bronchioles & alveoli,” but the shift begins at respiratory bronchioles; terminal bronchioles conduct air.
handling: Distinguish terminal bronchioles (conducting) from respiratory bronchioles (some exchange) and alveolar ducts/sacs.
